name: The Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem
statement: To capture a signal perfectly, sample it more than twice as fast as its highest frequency.
statementAccent: more than twice as fast as its highest frequency
meaning: A continuous signal that contains no frequencies above some limit can be reconstructed exactly from its samples, provided they are taken at a rate greater than twice that highest frequency. That threshold, twice the top frequency, is the Nyquist rate. Sample any slower and the fast components are irrecoverably corrupted.
mechanism: The signal must be band-limited, containing no energy above the cutoff, which real systems enforce with a low-pass anti-aliasing filter before sampling. Sample too slowly and frequencies above half the sampling rate fold back and masquerade as lower ones — aliasing — which cannot be undone afterward. When the criterion is met, the original is recovered exactly by sinc interpolation: each sample is weighted by an ideal interpolating kernel and the results summed, mathematically equivalent to ideal low-pass filtering.

examples.text: Human hearing tops out near twenty kilohertz, so audio must be sampled above forty; the compact disc uses 44.1 kilohertz, capturing up to about 22 and leaving a margin for real filters to roll off.
A rotating wheel filmed below twice its rotation rate appears to slow, stop, or spin backward — temporal aliasing, undersampling in time producing a false low frequency.
A sensor or screen sampling fine repeating detail more coarsely than twice its spatial frequency produces spurious patterns — spatial aliasing, countered with optical anti-aliasing filters.

variants.name: Nyquist rate versus Nyquist frequency
variants.text: Two often-confused thresholds — the Nyquist rate is twice the signal's top frequency, a property of the signal, while the Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate, a property of the sampler.

variants.name: Compressed sensing
variants.text: A modern qualifier showing that signals sparse in some domain can be recovered from far fewer samples than the theorem's sufficient condition demands, relaxing its assumptions rather than refuting it.

whyItMatters: It is the theoretical foundation of all digital signal processing, defining the bridge between the continuous analog world and discrete digital representation. Every recording, image, and communication that converts a wave into numbers rests on it, and it explains both why digital audio works and why aliasing artefacts appear when it is violated.

working.lead: Sample above twice the top frequency
working.text: to capture a signal faithfully, set the sampling rate above twice its highest frequency component.
apply an anti-aliasing low-pass filter first, since real signals are never perfectly band-limited.
distinguish the Nyquist rate, a property of the signal, from the Nyquist frequency, a property of your sampler.

limits: It requires strict band-limiting, an idealisation — a truly band-limited signal is infinite in time, so real signals are only approximately band-limited and need anti-aliasing filters, which have finite transition bands and motivate oversampling margins. The strict inequality matters: sampling at exactly twice the top frequency can miss content at the band edge. And compressed sensing shows the twice-the-highest-frequency bound is sufficient but not always necessary, since sparse signals can be recovered from fewer samples.
misreadings: It does not say you can never reconstruct an undersampled signal of any kind — under sparsity, sub-Nyquist recovery is possible; the theorem gives a sufficient condition, not the only one. And the Nyquist rate and Nyquist frequency are different quantities, one belonging to the signal and one to the sampler.
origin: Named for Harry Nyquist, whose 1928 work on telegraph transmission laid the groundwork, and Claude Shannon, who gave the formal statement and proof in 'Communication in the Presence of Noise' (1949); Vladimir Kotelnikov and E. T. Whittaker had reached equivalent results earlier.

sources.text: Shannon, C. (1949). “Communication in the Presence of Noise.” Proceedings of the IRE, vol. 37. — Shannon's statement of the sampling theorem.
Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, Wikipedia. — the statement, the Nyquist rate and frequency, aliasing, sinc reconstruction, and the discoverers.
"The origin story of the sampling theorem and Vladimir Kotelnikov," COMSOL Blog. — the multiple independent discoverers and Kotelnikov's 1933 formulation.
